title: The examen
hookLine: Ignatius taught a nightly look back: where was God today, where did I miss him?

cards: It's late. The house is quiet, and the mind starts its night shift, replaying the worst bits of the day. The awkward thing you said.

The email you shouldn't have sent. In 1521, in northern Spain, a young Basque soldier named Iñigo, proud, vain, in love with glory, has his leg smashed by a cannonball defending a fortress. For months he lies in bed.
He asks for adventure novels; the house has only a life of Christ and a book of saints' stories. Bored, he reads those, and notices something odd about his own daydreams.
That noticing will become a prayer practiced around the world.

teach.b: When he daydreamed about winning glory and impressing a great lady, it was exciting at the time, but afterward he felt dry and empty. When he daydreamed about living like the saints, the good feeling stayed.
He began to believe God was speaking through those after-feelings. The soldier became Ignatius of Loyola, founder of the Jesuits, and he wrote a manual for prayer called the Spiritual Exercises.
In it is a short daily practice called the examen, from the Latin for weighing, like the needle on a scale: a look back over the day, in five steps.
First, thanks for today's specific gifts. Second, ask for light, to see the day honestly. Third, walk back through the day, hour by hour: where was God in it?
Where did I feel alive, close, grateful? And where did I miss him, turn away, feel empty? Fourth, ask forgiveness for what needs it.
Fifth, look ahead to tomorrow with hope. Notice where it starts: not with what you did wrong, but with thanks. It isn't the bedtime replay of your worst moments.
It's a search for God in the ordinary hours, like the old prayer in the Psalms: "Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts."
The Jesuits have long told the story that Ignatius said his companions could skip other prayers on a busy day, but never the examen.
Catholics, Anglicans and many Protestants pray it too, usually at night, in about the time it takes to brush your teeth.
Its whole question fits in four words: where was he today?

how: Jesuits and many other Catholics pray the examen once or twice daily, often at night, and many Anglicans and Protestants use it too: giving thanks, asking for light, reviewing the day, asking forgiveness, and looking ahead to tomorrow.

o: a priest's test before someone is baptized
a list of sins read aloud before confession
a nightly prayer looking back over the day

games.q: the five steps — tap the pairs.
p: ask for light to see honestly
look ahead to tomorrow with hope

s: the examen is mainly a list of your sins
it starts with thanks, and looks for where God was in the day, before asking forgiveness.
Ignatius began to pray this way after a cannonball wound
recovering in bed, he noticed which daydreams left him empty and which left him at peace.
Catholics, Anglicans and many Protestants pray it too.

games.q: you're lying in bed at night, and your mind starts replaying the worst moments of the day. using the examen, where do you begin?
o: with the worst moment, to fix it.
games.why: Ignatius's examen begins with gratitude. only after thanks, and asking for light, do you review the day and ask forgiveness.

practice: Name one specific thing from today you're thankful for; if you pray, ask God to help you see honestly.
Rewind the day like a film, without judging, and stop on one moment where you felt most alive and one where you felt far away, or small.
If you pray, say sorry for what needs it and ask help for tomorrow; if you don't, just note what you've learned.

wordCard.voice: Examen: Ignatius's nightly look back, a weighing: thanks, light, review, sorry, and hope.

orig.note: Latin: the needle or tongue of a balance, a weighing. Ignatius's name for the daily review.

carryVoice: Your line: where was he today? Tomorrow, prayers that take three seconds. Sleep well tonight.
